explanations.answer: Where He did most of His miracles
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The text says Jesus began to denounce “…the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent.” Those towns got the most to see. The text says the trouble was that they did not repent.

I see why you'd go there, but the text never ties these cities to where John the Baptist preached. It says they're the cities “…in which most of His miracles had been performed…” The miracles are the link, so keep your eyes on those.

The Pharisees don't show up anywhere in these verses. Jesus is talking about cities, and what marks them is the miracles done there. The text says He denounces “…the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent.” That's all the passage gives us, so that's all I'll give you.

Right on the money. Jesus says that if those miracles had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, “…they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Tyre and Sidon were cities outside Israel. Notice He says long ago.

That's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says Tyre and Sidon, cities outside Israel, “…would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Nobody gets driven away in that sentence. They would have repented.

Nope, no extra signs on the order form. Jesus says the miracles done in Chorazin and Bethsaida were enough, because Tyre and Sidon “…would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Same miracles, different result. That's the whole point of what He's saying.

It's flipped, friend. Jesus says, “But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.” So the more bearable day goes to Tyre and Sidon, not to Chorazin and Bethsaida. This is a serious moment, so I'll just say it plainly.

You read that right. Jesus says, “But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.” The “you” is Chorazin and Bethsaida. It's a heavy line, and Jesus doesn't water it down.

That's it. Jesus asks Capernaum, “…will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!” It's a hard word, and the question He asks first makes the drop even bigger. I think this one stings.

Egypt is a fine place for a road trip, but Jesus never says it here. He says, “…will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!” The word is Hades. It's a heavy word, so it's worth reading carefully.

Babylon doesn't come up in these verses. After asking Capernaum if it will be lifted up to heaven, Jesus says, “No, you will be brought down to Hades!” That's the word the blank is waiting for. It's a hard line, so it's good to see it exactly as He said it.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day.” Sodom is the city the LORD rained sulfur and fire on (Genesis 19:24). So the Lord of those miracles is saying Sodom would still be standing if it had seen what Capernaum saw.

This one is actually true, and it's a surprising one. Jesus says, “For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day.” Sodom is the city the LORD rained sulfur and fire on (Genesis 19:24). So He's saying that with Capernaum's miracles, Sodom would still be around.

Yes! Jesus says, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.” Good news for a stamper with no diploma. The ones who receive it are little children.

Close, but that's not who Jesus names. He says the Father has “…hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.” Priests aren't mentioned in the verse. Little children are.

No advisors in this verse, friend. Jesus says the Father has “…hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.” The ones who receive it are little children. I find that encouraging, since I never got a title either.

That's what He says. Jesus says, “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” Knowing the Father comes through the Son. That's a big deal for every baker who wants to know God.

This one is true, so you can trust it. Jesus says, “…no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” The Son is the One who reveals Him. It's right there in verse 27.
That's the promise! Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” Notice He says all of you who are weary and burdened. Nobody is left off the list.

Riches would be nice when the bills show up, but that's not the promise. Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” For the weary and burdened, He offers rest.

Victory sounds great, but it's not what Jesus offers in this verse. He says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” The word is rest. And it goes to anyone who is weary and burdened.
Yes, friend. Jesus says, “…I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” He describes His own heart. That's what you get when you come to Him and learn from Him.

That sounds like a movie poster, but it's not how Jesus describes Himself here. He says, “…I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” He chose gentle and humble. Those are His own words about Himself.

Tireless would be nice for a stamper who gets worn down, but that's not the verse. Jesus says, “…I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” He talks about His heart, not His body. Gentle and humble is the answer.
That's it. Jesus says, “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.” Those are His words for what He asks us to carry. It's a good way to end His invitation.
That's a reasonable thing to expect, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.” Light is the word He uses for His burden. Heavy doesn't show up.
I can see why you'd guess it, but Jesus says something different. He says, “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.” He says easy, not hard. And He says nothing about how long it lasts.
